newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Invisible funds gaining influence in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Invisible funds gaining influence in Asia.

text.p: Large-scale financial flows have assumed huge influence in Asia but many of the projects they are backing remain invisible, delegates to World Economic Forum Europe/Asia summit were told on Wednesday.

A culture clash between Asian business that had traditionally relied on family investors and North American fund managers unfamiliar with Asia had resulted in something of a stalemate, financial experts said at the 1996 Europe/East Asia Summit organised by the World Economic Forum.

Frustrated by Asia's lack of transparency and unsophisticated markets, foreign institutions were quietly pooling capital into private funds that invested directly in infrastructure projects and private companies.

"These deals are very rarely announced and when they are they don't tend necessarily to gain a big profile and they don't take place in any particularly visible marketplace," said Timothy Beardson, chairman of Crosby Financial Holdings in Hong Kong.
"These funds are taking minority positions in businesses across this entire region. These money managers conduct their business in a very professional way, but not necessarily a very visible way."
But Asian markets were sufficiently sophisticated to attract substantial portfolio flows that some Asian nations were starting to view with increasing distrust.

"International fund managers are so important these days, they can pull governments down," said Narongchai Akrasanee, chairman and chief executive officer of Thailand's General and Securities Company.

Thailand's attempt to lure foreign investment through special tax treatment of short-term debt and a lucrative interest rate arbitrage prompted a downgrade of the country's short-term debt ratings and significant economic instability.
Akrasanee said that in Asia, finding money was easy. Finding the right kind of money, however, was more difficult.

Beardson said bonds were an obvious alternative for a region expected to require infrastructure spending of US$1.5 trillion over the next few years, but there were few signs that World Bank forecasts of an Asian bond market valued at US$1 trillion by 2005 would materialise any time soon.

Working against its development were an Asian fondness for equity and loans and an unfamiliarity with bonds, Beardson said, even though growing pools of retirement savings in North America were desperate to exploit Asia's growth potential.
Financial experts had an obligation to promote the nature of Asian business more effectively to fund managers, but Asian businesses must also do their part, he said.

"Asian businesses need to go further down the road to making their accounting more transparent, presenting themselves more articulately, providing better investor relations, if they wish to attract what are substantially growing potential sources of capital," he said.
